blocks.text: Returning to the document, members of the jury, section 4, "Pathology", and agreed fact number 20, which refers to [Baby A], date of birth 7 June 2015:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "(i) Dr Rajeev Shukla, consultant paediatric pathologist, conducted a post-mortem examination of [Baby A] at the Royal Liverpool Children's Hospital (Alder Hey) at 12.30 hours on 10 June 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "(ii) Dr Shukla made a written report of the examination dated 14 September 2015, which included the following findings of fact.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Cardiovascular system: The pulmonary trunk arises normally. However, the pulmonary arteries are crossed with the left pulmonary artery originating to the right and above the origin of the right pulmonary artery. Foramen ovale is patent.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Respiratory system: The lungs are severely congested and haemorrhagic.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Microscopy: Multiple sections from the lungs show marked capillary congestion and congestive collapse of the alveoli."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The glossary you'll receive, members of the jury, may inform you, as you may very well know, that the alveoli are tiny air sacs within the lungs that allow gas exchange.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Continuing with this paragraph:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Foci of intra-alveolar haemorrhage is noted."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: to foci, members of the jury, focus is a pathological term describing -- surrounding tissues based on their appearance. I can see the version of the glossary I'm using is --
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: It needs amendment.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. I'm just using the wrong version. You'll receive the definitions in due course:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The alveolar ducts appear dilated and contain squames indicating amniotic fluid aspiration. There is no obvious meconium or inflammation. There are no viral conclusions.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Toxicology: The toxicological investigation showed caffeine in concentrations consistent with therapeutic use. There was no other toxicological abnormality to explain sudden unexpected death of this infant."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Conclusions. Dr Shukla noted that:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The only positive finding was that of crossed pulmonary arteries. Dr Shukla observed that crossed pulmonary arteries are
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: a quite rare form of pulmonary arterial malposition. It has been described in association with congenital cardiac and extracardiac diseases. No other anomalies were noted in this case. In absence of any other abnormality, it is unlikely to be significant as a cause of death."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Shukla observed that:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "There is a strong temporal relationship between the long line insertion and the patient's apnoeic spell and collapse. The long line's position could not be confirmed at autopsy as it was removed during life."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The next agreed fact, that is to say agreed fact number 21, relates to the baby [Baby C], date of birth, 10 June 2015:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "(i) Dr George Kokai, consultant paediatric pathologist, conducted a post-mortem examination of [Baby C] at Royal Liverpool Children's Hospital (Alder Hey) at 10.00 hours on 16 June 2015."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Kokai made a written report of the examination dated 25 September 2015, which included the following findings of fact:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Abdominal cavity: All abdominal organs show normal anatomical position. The gallbladder, extrahepatic biliary ducts and pancreas are normal. The stomach and all loops of bowel and mesentery show normal rotation pattern apart from descending colon, which crosses the midline into the right lower abdominal cavity and connects to the sigmoid colon, which is in normal position. The serosal cover is thin, shiny and translucent. The stomach contains a large amount of air and some bile-stained secretions. The remaining bowel is empty. The colon contains meconium.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Lungs: Saccular stage of development with partial atelectasis areas of fresh bleeding into interstitium and distal airways. Also, multiple areas of partly resolving hyaline membrane in many foci without inflammation. Foetal type of wall of pulmonary arterial bed with patent lumina. Congested pulmonary venous bed."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That's classically a paragraph that's going to have to be explained to us by Dr Marnerides, what all that means.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Understood.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Agreed fact number 22 relates to the baby [Baby D]. Date of birth 20 June 2015:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "(i) Dr Jo McPartland, consultant paediatric pathologist, conducted a post-mortem examination of [Baby D] at the Royal Liverpool Children's Hospital (Alder Hey) at 11.15 hours on 23 June 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "(ii) Dr McPartland made written reports of the examination dated 3 August 2017 and 13 May 2019, which included the following findings of fact.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "(a) In her report of 3 August 2017 Dr McPartland observed that:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Lungs: There is patchy acute pneumonia, most prominent within one of the right lung samples with some hyaline membranes present, indicating diffuse alveolar damage. Although pneumonia can develop secondary to ventilation, the period of intubation and ventilation was short in this case, taking into account the clinical scenario with spontaneous rupture of membranes 36 hours before birth."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: to that 36 hours before birth you'll read in due course Dr McPartland qualifies that later, but just reading as per her first report:
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "... with spontaneous rupture of membranes 36 hours before birth, and then collapse of the baby soon after birth followed by continuing respiratory problems and the histological pneumonia, which is quite convincing, I think it is likely that pneumonia was already present at birth.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "It is most unfortunate that the placenta was disposed of after delivery as examination may have revealed an ascending genital tract infection as the cause of congenital pneumonia and would have allowed me to be more definitive about the timing of onset of the pneumonia.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "Although [Baby D]'s CRP was low, in early onset sepsis the sensitivity of CRP in detecting infection may be as low as 22% and therefore does not rule out infection. Microbiology tests were negative in this case, but this is often the case after antibiotic treatment and does not rule out infection, which is histologically proven in this case.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "Virology tests were negative for viral infections. Toxicology revealed a very low concentration of morphine consistent with that routinely used in neonatal care during intubation and ventilation."
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Dr McPartland also recorded the following summary findings:
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "(i) Early neonatal death after 36 hours of age.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "(ii) A normally growth (sic) and developed baby girl with weight on the 91st percentile. Length on 25th percentile and head circumference on the 98th percentile.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "(iii) Acute pneumonia with hyaline membranes indicating alveolar damage.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "(iv) Placenta not submitted for examination."
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So paragraph (b). In her report of 13 May 2019, Dr McPartland observed that:
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "After issuing my post-mortem examination report, I was informed by Dr J Davies, consultant obstetrician at the Countess of Chester Hospital, that the duration of premature rupture of membranes was 60 hours, not 36 hours, as I had stated in my report."
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: That's obviously a reference back to the top line of that page where it says 60 hours, which I've scrubbed through and written 36.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Vice versa, my Lord. The top of the page reads 36 hours --
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Members of the jury, the next agreed fact, agreed fact number 23, relates to the baby [Baby I], date of birth 7 August 2015:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "(i) Dr George Kokai, consultant paediatric pathologist, conducted a post-mortem examination of [Baby I] at the Royal Liverpool Children's Hospital (Alder Hey) at 14.30 hours on 26 October 2015. (ii) Dr Kokai made a written report of the examination dated 25 September 2017."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The next agreed fact, agreed fact number 24, relates to the baby [Baby O], date of birth 21 June 2016:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "(i) Dr George Kokai, consultant paediatric pathologist, conducted a post-mortem examination of [Baby O] at the Royal Liverpool Children's Hospital (Alder Hey) at 14.00 hours on 28 June 2016. Dr Kokai made a written report of the examination dated 25 September 2017."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Agreed fact number 24 relates to the baby [Baby P], date of birth 21 June 2016:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "(i) Dr George Kokai, consultant paediatric pathologist, conducted a post-mortem examination of [Baby P] at the Royal
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Liverpool Children's Hospital (Alder Hey) at 15.00 hours on 28 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "(ii) Dr Kokai made a written report of the examination dated 25 September 2017."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Agreed fact number 25:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "No post-mortem examination was conducted of [Baby E] or [Baby K]."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: My Lord, may I hand over to Mr Johnson?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Andreas Marnerides, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: DR ANDREAS MARNERIDES (affirmed)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Thank you very much. I wonder whether you'd like to take a seat.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We have a live transcript being kept of the proceedings, so if you wouldn't mind just pulling the microphone towards you to make sure that what you say can be heard.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Could we start by you telling the jury who you are, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I'm Dr Andreas Kyriacou Marnerides and I'm a consultant perinatal and paediatric pathologist based at St Thomas' Hospital in London.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Thank you. That's a bit of a mouthful. Could you just explain -- I'll come to your qualifications in a moment, doctor, but could you explain to the jury what your day-to-day work involves, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So a pathologist is a medical doctor that has trained in a specialty called pathology. That's a specialty that means basically two things of expertise: one is interpreting specimens from the living, biopsies that you may have heard, so if somebody had an operation, they're being investigated for a tumour or any other disease, the pathologist will look at that specimen under the microscope and help the clinicians make the diagnosis. The other part of their expertise is when they perform post-mortem examinations, so people that have died.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: A perinatal and paediatric pathologist has the sub-specialty of dealing with the paediatric population.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: The term perinatal refers to the time around a woman's pregnancy and the early time after the baby's delivered.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So the perinatal pathologist has the expertise in examining the placentas in case there is a need for examination, foetuses that have died in utero, so before they were born, babies that are born alive and die very early in the neonatal period. And of course the paediatric, you can understand, is every age of a child.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Thank you. In terms of your workload, doctor, how many cases of perinatal and paediatric people do you deal with a year?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So in terms of post-mortem examinations, at my department we do roughly 750 post-mortem perinatal/paediatric examinations. This includes both cases that are -- those that are called hospital cases, so there is -- the doctors and the parents want to investigate further what has happened in the pregnancy or why there was a stillborn baby or the baby died early in their life. There is no coronial, so no judge involved, and no police involvement.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: But we also do, which is a big number -- around half of these cases, the 750, are medico-legal cases, so there is a coronial request or a police request. I'm dealing with 99% of those requests that have come through the police, so the forensic cases where there's a suspected crime being investigated.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: It's three pathologists that do the 750, three consultant pathologists, so I would be roughly doing one third. And on Fridays we go through the cases that we have seen and discuss all the cases, so even if one has not done the post-mortem examination, one has the experience of what the other colleagues have seen in that post-mortem examination, what were the findings, and then there is a discussion around that.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So your figure of 750, is that a year?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's a year.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Okay. In very round terms, about two a day in very round terms?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I can't do the maths as quickly as you.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: You're more likely to get to the right answer than I am!
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It depends what you call a day. Days of the calendar, yes, but the working days, unless you're working 7 days a week carrying out post-mortems, it's...
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We can all understand the mathematics.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: All right. So that's your day-to-day working life.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Could we deal with your qualifications, please? Can we take these reasonably slowly, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. So I have a medical degree from the Medical School of the University of Athens in Greece.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: In what year did you get your medical degree?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So 21 years ago?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Then I proceeded with training -- in Greece it's called forensic medicine, it's the equivalent of forensic pathology in the United Kingdom. I did a PhD as well in pathology: I studied the function of Hodgkin's lymphoma, which is a haematological malignancy, so a tumour of the blood in very simple terms. Then I proceeded and I went to the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm and did my training in paediatric and perinatal pathology.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: I joined St Thomas' Hospital as a consultant perinatal and paediatric pathologist in January 2013, having worked for approximately a year as a consultant before that in Sweden. And since then I'm based at the St Thomas' -- since 2013 I'm based at St Thomas'. The everyday work is what I have described before that.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: I became a fellow of the Royal College of Pathologists, I think it was 2021, and I also hold the diploma of medical jurisprudence, which is -- from the Royal Society of Apothecaries in London, which is specialising in forensic pathology.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: For anyone that doesn't know St Thomas' Hospital in London, is that one of the main teaching hospitals in the capital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Thank you. What I'd like to do, doctor, is to go through the cases that you can help us with one by one, if we may. There are two lever arch files in front of you and the one to the left has a number 1 on it.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Behind divider 3 are some agreed facts. If you go to agreed fact 20 onwards, please. These have just been read to the jury, just before you came in. What I'd like you to do, please, is to help us as to what these mean.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Agreed fact 20 mentions a baby by the name of [Baby A]. [Baby A]'s case is one of the ones that you have reviewed; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: We see that a Dr Rajeev Shukla, who is a consultant paediatric pathologist in Liverpool, conducted a post-mortem examination of [Baby A] at Alder Hey Hospital at 12.30 hours on 10 June 2015 and that he issued a written report dated 14 September.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: He made the following findings of fact on his examination -just before we get to the details of this, when a post-mortem examination is conducted by a pathologist, does it start with a description of what's on the outside of the body?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So a post-mortem examination in babies starts even before the description of what one sees on the outside of the baby. It typically starts with a post-mortem radiology examination. That's either X-rays that are taken at the mortuary with a machine called a Faxitron, to which the pathologist has direct access. This is typically the case in so-called hospital cases when there is no involvement of coroners or the police. And in that case, the pathologist has the training to assess the growth of the skeleton, that's the reason of doing the examination, and whether there is anything that would suggest that there is an underlying metabolic bone disease for that baby.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: If it is a medico-legal post-mortem examination then the radiology examination is much more detailed, it's called a skeletal survey, and that is being reported according to the guidelines by a paediatric radiologist, so a radiologist that has sub-specialty or is working in a paediatric hospital.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So even before examining externally, this is what's happening. When the pathologist goes in the post-mortem examination room, the pathologist will make an examination of how the baby or the child looks externally. They will typically take some measurements and weigh the baby to assist them in forming an
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: opinion on what's the baby's growth, whether they're growing normally or not, using those parameters. And on the external examination, they will look for dysmorphic features of the case.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: What does dysmorphic means?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It means that something has not formed in the way we expect it to form. So for example, we expect the ears of the baby to be set at the level we are used to seeing them in everyone. If they are low set, so set below where we typically expect them, that's called low set ears and that's a dysmorphic feature. So that's one thing all pathologists will look for. They will look at everything else, so the trunk, the front and the back of the body, the limbs, the fingers, the genitalia, the anus, everything that is visible from the outside, and see whether everything has formed the way it should have formed.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: They will also typically, in cases where there is a coronial or police involvement, note down whether there are any injuries visible from the outside, note down whether they see marks of medical intervention, so needles, needle puncture marks, cannulas, tubes, they will write those down.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: In many -- not all, many -- we will make a detailed or less detailed assessment of how the post-mortem phenomena have developed. The post-mortem phenomena is what -- in layman's terms we say decomposition. This goes -- we decompose in stages. So some pathologists will be more detailed in that, some will be less detailed in that, and some will just not say anything at all.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So once the pathologist has assessed the outside of the body following the radiological investigation, does the examination then proceed to what is inside the body?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Sometimes before that, the pathologist may take some samples for testing before even opening the body, so may take some swabs from the nose or from the mouth or take a small piece of skin for some tests that we need to do. Then we will proceed with opening the body cavities.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: A typical way of doing this -- and I apologise, I understand this is distressing, but this is how it's done -- there is an incision typically starting from the upper part of the chest going down to the lower abdomen and then they will expose the organs of the baby.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: The first check done there is: is every organ where it's supposed to be, does it look the way it should?
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: And then they will make a dissection of each organ to assess the anatomy of the organs, weigh them, if there is a need, take photographs, either in situ, so inside the body, or when they take them outside of the body, and take small pieces of tissue from the organs to look.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Those will be processed in the lab so we get slides that we can look under the microscope and make an assessment on the microscopic level, so on the cellular level.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Then after finishing with the organs of the chest and the abdomen and the structures of the neck, the brain is being removed from the head. So the scalp is reflected and checked, the anatomy of the skull bones is checked, the brain is removed. Typically the brain will have to be fixed in a liquid, which is called formalin, because if you try to examine a baby's brain in particular, in a fresh state, the information you will get is not very useful because they go into autolysis very quickly and the brains of babies, once you put an incision through them, typically will start melting and you can't really examine them. So we fix them and we examine them at a later stage and take the samples then.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: By fixing in this context is it literally put the brain into a liquid, formalin, that you have said?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Does it harden the brain?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's what it does: it makes it harder so we can make incisions and assess the anatomy.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes. We will come to some details relating to that perhaps in the case of [Baby A]. But just continuing with the process for now, just taking up what you have said about the organs, when we get to the cases of the [Surname of Babies O, P & R] brothers, [Baby O] and [Baby P], will we be hearing from you that they had unusual findings in their livers?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: In order for you to explain to us those particular findings, are there some photographs of their livers?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: In order for you properly to explain to the jury what the findings are and your conclusions, will it be necessary to show the jury those photographs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In my opinion, yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: This is never pleasant, everybody understands that. But is the position that the photography focuses solely on the liver?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: And so there's no picture of either child as one would normally see a child?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, it's only the liver.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now can we take up the case first of [Baby A], please, Dr Marnerides. You can see there on the page in front of you are some agreed facts that have been read to the jury this morning.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'd like you just to give us a few words of explanation, if you would. So we see the first underlined heading in paragraph 20 is "Cardiovascular system". What is that a reference to in terms of the anatomy, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's a reference to the heart and the vessels.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: And the vessels are what?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The major vessels that one can access and examine in a baby are the vessels that originate from the heart and the vessels that end to the heart. The vessels that originate from the heart are called arteries. The major artery that originates from the heart and gives blood supply to everything in our body, basically, is called -- it has a specific name and it's called the aorta. So that's the one major vessel that leaves the heart and it's called the aorta. The other major vessel that leaves -takes away blood from the heart is called the pulmonary artery and it takes blood to the lungs; that's why it's called pulmonary. Where that blood -- there will be an oxygenation of
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: the blood and the blood will return to the heart via the pulmonary veins.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So the vessels bringing, back from the body, blood to the heart are called veins. So the blood coming back to the heart from the lungs are the pulmonary veins.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: From the rest of the body it's the superior vena cava, so the big vessel that brings back blood from the upper part of the body, to put it as simply as possible, and the inferior vena cava brings blood back from the lower part of the body.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: These are the vessels that are always examined. In some occasions, when the anatomy allows it and the size of the vessels and the instruments we have access to allow it, a pathologist may be more meticulous or interested in examining smaller vessels in the periphery of the body. Those I referred to have always been examined.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: All right. We see, just going back to the written word on the page for a moment:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "The pulmonary trunk arises normally."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What does that mean, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's the main of the proximal -- so the heart has four chambers, two atria and two ventricles; two are on the right side and two are on the left side. The blood circulation, so you can understand it, comes from the rest of the body into the right atrium, goes into the right ventricle. From the right ventricle arises the pulmonary trunk, which is the small proximal part of the vessel I referred to, the pulmonary artery. Remember?
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: That vessel has two branches, the left and right pulmonary artery, and those take blood to the lungs.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "The pulmonary trunk arises normally", what does that mean?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That means it was arising from the pulmonary valve, which is at the right place in the right ventricle.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Thank you:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "However [recorded Dr Shukla], the pulmonary arteries are crossed with the left pulmonary artery originating to the right and above the origin of the right pulmonary artery."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So what does that mean in practical terms?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So imagine that you have a tube and you get a branch from the tube that goes to the left, a branch from the tube that goes to the right. That's the normal branching of the pulmonary trunk. In this occasion, the branch that was originating from the left was turning and going to the right and the branch originating from the right was turning and going to the left.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So this is a finding that can be seen in isolation or can be seen in association with other malformations of the heart. In this instance it was seen in isolation. When it's seen in isolation, it's not known to have any clinical consequences to the individual.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: The best example for that is that we see it as an incidental finding even in adults that have survived many years, no issues whatsoever, because they didn't have anything else with that.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: If there is a malformation then we are discussing a different thing, but in this case there was no associated malformation to make anyone worried that this could not be regarded within the variation of normality.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Next:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Foramen ovale is patent."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The jury have heard a bit about this, but if you could give us the forensic pathologist's point of view, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So if you remember, we said there are four chambers in the heart, the two upper are called the atria, the two lower are called the ventricles. In between them there is a septum, a wall, if I put it simply. The wall, the septum, between the left and the right atrium has a round structure called the fossa ovale. That's a Latin term for saying that it's a round area, that's how it's translated.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: This fossa ovale in the intrauterine life has a membranous covering which is called a septum, which functions like a flap. You need to have communication in the intrauterine life between the two atria.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: When babies are being born, this will not close anatomically within the first period of life. It will typically close later on in their life, but some individuals will have a small opening there in the fossa ovale, anatomically open, and this may become a problem later on in their life.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: In a newborn baby or a few months' old baby, an anatomically open foramen ovale, patent foramen ovale, is what we expect to see.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Next in the written word, please:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Respiratory system: the lungs are severely congested and haemorrhagic."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What does that mean, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It literally means that the pathologist that looked at the lungs and felt that they were more -- apologies for the word I will be using -- contain more blood on their cut surfaces than what he would expect to see. Okay?
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: That's what it literally means.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: If you're asking me what it means as a finding, what's the pertinence of the finding in relation to the cause of death, the answer is it basically means nothing because it's a very common finding, a very non-specific finding. That's the reason people take histology to look under the microscope to see whether that impression they had on a naked-eye examination has any pertinence or not.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So histology, we're back to taking samples --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: -- tissue samples which are preserved, stained, put on a slide and looked at under a microscope?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So that description, "The lungs are severely congested and haemorrhagic", is that what you would call a macroscopic observation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, a naked-eye observation.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Thank you. That's probably why we go to microscopy next. So macroscopy, lungs severely congested and haemorrhagic, in other words the naked-eye view. Viewed through the microscope, it says:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Multiple sections from the lungs..."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In this context, are sections the samples that are put on to slides and looked at under the microscope?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "... show marked capillary congestion and congestive collapse of the alveoli."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Could you put that into language I can understand?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: To put things into context, a baby's lung would be about this size each, the whole lung (indicating).
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: About the size of, what, a plum?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: A plum, yes, maybe slightly bigger. The right lung has three lobes, so imagine this size (indicating) divided in three. The left lung has two lobes, so divided into two.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: On microscopy, you cut through those lobes and you take a small piece of tissue, which is not thicker than maybe half a centimetre in thickness, and not bigger than this (indicating), so maybe a couple of centimetres. This is put in a plastic container, which is slightly bigger than 2 centimetres, and the sections we get after the processing you described are of the thickness of 4 microns. So divide the millimetres -- the thickness of our hair, okay? That thickness, of a hair. So that's what we look at in the microscope.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: It's that level of examination.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Capillaries are the very, very, very small vessels, the most distal part of our circulation. Those were seen by the pathology as markedly congested. So typically, you expect to see some of those capillaries full of blood, some empty. His assessment was that he saw more of the capillaries being full of blood rather than the proportion of empty and full of blood typically seen. That's the congestion of the capillaries.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "Congestive collapse of the alveoli." So the structure of the lung is -- if you imagine minute balloons within very, very small structures, that's where the air that we breathe goes from the larynx, the trachea and the bronchi into those small air spaces, small balloons that you can only see under the microscope; they're very, very small. Those are typically filled with air. When he says "congestive collapse of the alveoli", he says that instead of seeing them open like this (indicating), next to areas where the small capillaries were full of blood, he saw them collapsed. That's the description of what he saw.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: The next line says:
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: "Foci of intra-alveolar haemorrhage is noted."
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So he says that in those small spaces where one knows air should be, he saw blood, haemorrhage.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Thank you. We go on then to:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "The alveolar ducts appeared dilated and contain squames, indicating amniotic fluid aspiration."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So the alveolar ducts is a descriptive term used as synonymous to the alveoli. Okay? So these air spaces have a cellular lining. They're called pneumocytes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: When we look at lungs from dead babies we know that some of those pneumocytes will start disintegrating and collapsing into that empty space and they form squames, that's what we call them, so flakes of tissue that doesn't really have a cellular component or a nuclear component that we can say, "Yes, this is a dead pneumocyte".
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: But also in babies we know that, in utero, the way the lung is growing is by the fluid within which the baby lives in the womb of his or her mother -- swallows/aspirates that fluid because that's the normal thing to do, that's how the lungs grow in utero. You need that. So some remnants of that is what Dr Shukla describes that he saw. And it's a normal thing to see in this setting. It's nothing.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Then finally so far as this paragraph is concerned:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "There is no obvious meconium or inflammation."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Are we still talking about the lungs here?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We're still talking about the lungs. So he's making this comment to say -- so it's a normal process for the lung, for that fluid ending into the lungs, okay, in utero. But sometimes when babies get stressed in utero they discharge meconium. Meconium is the baby's stool.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: If the baby then aspirates that meconium because it's in the fluid, this could be used as a sign, not make the diagnosis, but it's a sign that the pathologist would need to assess if they see it, to say was this baby stressed in utero or not.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Inflammation is the body's response to external stressors, the most common in this setting being infection, so an infection either inside the womb or outside the womb. The pathologist tells us that he did not see any reaction to such a thing, so he has nothing to tell him that there had been any source of infection.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The other term is, "There are no viral inclusions". The last sentence. Viral infections in babies is a topic of interest in all perinatal and paediatric pathologists because we know that such infections can result to intrauterine death, so stillbirth, or early neonatal death. So we're trained and we meticulously always look for signs of such an infection, a viral infection.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: There are two major categories of signs. One is whether you see viral inclusions, so the virus bodies themselves inside the cells, and he couldn't see those.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: The other way of testing for that, for looking for that on histology, is whether you see inflammatory response, the type of the response expected in viral infections.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: That type of response is different to what one sees in bacterial infections. One is characterised, the bacteria, by neutrophils, the other is characterised typically by lymphocytes, but he says he didn't see any inflammation, so that includes both bacterial and viral.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Does that translate in simple terms then to no evidence of infection?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: I'm sorry to break this down, but "spherical empty spaces or globules", what does that mean, what are you seeing?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So structures that resemble a grape that has been cut through and you only see one surface of that cut, so round
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: or roughly round structures. But I see them on two dimensions, so a section, not in three dimensions.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Imagine a grape, cutting through it, and that surface you get, looking on it from the top, that's a spherical structure.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Where did you see those spherical empty spaces or globules?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Within the lumens of small -- of medium-sized veins. So the lungs, remember this big (indicating), cut on very thin layers. They have veins and arteries. And the veins -- you can tell the difference most of the times within an artery and a vein on the microscopic level.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: And those veins, imagine tubes, cut through them, you have a ring. So the inside of the ring is called the lumen. In those lumens, in the inside of the ring, the ring being the vein, on the inside of the ring I saw that cut surface that resembled the cut surface of a grape.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: If we think of a vein as being a tunnel, you're looking down the tunnel from end to end?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: That view. And as you look down the tunnel, you see a round object in the tunnel?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. But that's three-dimensional, I'm looking two dimensions. So I'm looking at a section like this (indicating) of the tunnel.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes. And what was the significance of what you could see to your trained eye?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Those empty spaces, which meant that they stained for neither haematoxylin, which is the substance we use, or eosin, which is the other substance we use, had no colour, they were white.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: What does blood show up as in a vein if you stain it with haematoxylin or the other substance?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We stained the slide with both, haematoxylin and eosin.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: The blood will look red and you see red blood cells and you see the other cellular components of the blood, for example neutrophils, which have a different -- they have a bluish multilobulated nucleus and a red surrounding.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: You see lymphocytes, which have basically no surrounding but a very dark, round nucleus. You see the different structures. This was an empty structure, a white structure. And in practice, this can be two things: it can either be air or it can be fat. Okay?
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Fat has a slightly different appearance from -- so the empty space we typically see when it's fat, it's different to the grape structure that I have described.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: It's much smaller, so it's not a grape, it's a small berry, if you compare the sizes, that has been cut.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: It's typically round rather than oval or spherical or multilobulated, that could be air. Plus when we see fat, we always look -- when we think it's fat and we see something, a small globule and we think it's fat, we look for further evidence of fat embolism because that's when you expect to see fat.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: When do we get fat embolus? We get it when we have a fractured bone. And when we have that, it's because small fragments of the bone will get into the circulation and go into the vessels.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: When we see fat emboli, we will, with very careful observation, find next to those globules in other vessels or in capillaries, elements of bone marrow. In this case I didn't see the globules that I would expect to see if this was fat.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So they were not typical of fat globules?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, and I did not see the other elements of bone marrow embolism -- plus we had no fractures that would explain why we had these (inaudible).
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So what conclusion did you draw as to --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I need to say something else.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Sorry, I beg your pardon.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So if these blocks were sent to me a decade ago, I would have requested from the lab to undertake a special stain, the single special stain we can on paraffin-embedded tissue called osmium stain, that specifically stains fat, and I would have excluded that possibility. However, it's a very toxic substance, labs don't do it anymore, so we can't do that. What we do nowadays, not having the -- not being allowed to use that stain anymore, basically, because there are health risks for the lab staff, we take smaller pieces from the tissues of interest,
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: routinely, we freeze them, and those can be stained with -- but it needs to be frozen tissue, which we didn't have here. It needs to be stained with a stain called Oil Red O and that will give us the answer whether indeed it's fat or not.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So from what I had, my conclusion was that this would more likely than not -- these spaces represent air.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I saw a similar thing in a section from the brain, in that I could see that the lumen was surrounded by blood, which tells me, but I cannot be 100% sure, I cannot be categoric, it tells me that most likely this bubble of air went there while this baby was alive because there is a response to that. And the response is the haemorrhage.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So in the brain, air in the brain or gas in the brain?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's how it looked.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: And there was a response to the air, which suggested that that air went to the brain in life?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. However, I need to make it clear to this court and to the jurors that those findings cannot be taken as an absolute proof.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They are in my eyes and my opinion suggestive, highly suggestive, but if I had no other history, no clinical information, no assessment by a clinician, and I only had those two findings, I would have said, "I cannot really tell you if it's air there and it's not an artefact explicable on the decomposition changes and all the artefacts we made".
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Does it come to this, that you cannot say, and you do not say, that your findings necessarily mean that there was an air embolism in this case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Would it be fair to say that one has to look at other evidence to make that determination, if there is any other evidence?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If there is any evidence, the pathologist needs to take that into account. We need to accept that a post-mortem examination is a snapshot, taken after the death of an individual, of the process of somebody dying. So to interpret
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: the snapshot, sometimes we are able to say without any clinical information, "Yes, this is what I see, this is what happened", but in many cases, and that's the bread and butter of paediatric pathology, we need the assessment of the course before that snapshot.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: If that assessment tells me that the findings indicate towards air embolus being the case, my findings would be consistent with that. But my findings on their own would not say yes it is.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: We've heard from Professor Arthurs, the radiologist, about gas getting into the circulation after death. Was there any evidence from what was seen at the post-mortem examination, the pathologist's examination, to suggest that decomposition likely played a part in any gas in the bloodstream?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, there wasn't. It's highly unlikely.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Highly unlikely. Why do you say that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because for decomposition to result in air into vessels, you need to have evidence of decomposition. This evidence of decomposition is typically visible to the naked eye, so you see decomposing bowels, you see a greenish discolouration of the abdomen. Most importantly, on histology, so looking under the microscope, the structures look autolysed and you can say, yes, there has been significant decomposition here or not; this was not the case here.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: The other reason is that the brain -- there was a response to that finding that wouldn't -- the haemorrhage around that vessel. That wouldn't be expected if that was due to decomposition. So although one cannot categorically say it wasn't, I think I would confidently say it's highly unlikely.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: There's one thing I have overlooked as we've gone through and that's the issue of a tamponade, which is to do with the long line perforating or agitating against the heart. blocks.text: Can you direct me to where I deal with this?

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's what Dr Evans assessed.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Forget that then.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If there was evidence of tamponade at post-mortem, one would have seen haemorrhage into the sac that surrounds the heart; that's called the pericardium. One would have seen blood there. Dr Shukla did not see blood there and there was no such blood in the photographs.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes. So what Dr Shukla recorded as the physical findings and what you have seen from the photographs do not support any suggestion that there was tamponade?

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Thank you.

blocks.text: Can we go to the opinion section, please, of your report, Dr Marnerides. Was there any evidence of any natural disease in [Baby A] that could have contributed to his premature death?

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I just want to show you a picture that has been produced earlier in the case. It's D8, I believe.

blocks.text: Thank you.

blocks.text: I'd be very grateful if you would.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Where my cursor is, that's where the stomach is (indicating). The next part is called the duodenum; that's the first segment of our small bowel. This continues into the
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: abdomen. In the central part of our abdomen, roughly, is the small bowel, the loops of the small bowel; they are called jejunum, it's the part of the duodenum. The ileum is the distal part of the small bowel; this connects typically to the large bowel on the lower right-hand side part of our abdomen to the caecum, which is the first part of the large bowel or the colon, that's the other name. That's where many people may be familiar -- that's where the appendix is, so people may be familiar with that.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then the colon has an upwards direction to turn. That turning point is called hepatic flexure because it turns at the level of the liver, which, to give you an understanding, if you put your right hand on the end of your ribs, that's where approximately your belly starts, that's where approximately this turn happens. That's where your liver is.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Then it goes on a transverse way in front of the stomach, so not entirely how it's shown in the photograph. It goes in front of the stomach. That's called the transverse colon. On the lefthand side of the abdomen, so this side on your body where the spleen is, it's called the splenic flexure, it turns downwards.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: The downwards-going part of the colon is called the descending colon. And around the level of where your umbilicus is, where your belly button is, on the left-hand side, slightly below that, the pattern that we see of the colon resembles the S letter -- that's why it's called the sigmoid because it resembles the S -- to come and meet the part of the colon which is the most distal part called the rectum, and that's where it connects with the anus and that's the opening of our colon.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Right. So that's a description. What we see here in the written word is that:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "[The abnormality] [the descending colon] crosses the midline into the right lower abdominal cavity and connects to the sigmoid colon, which is in the normal position."

blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So instead of being all the way on the left-hand side, you have the bowel forming something like this (indicating) and then it continues downwards in a normal way.

blocks.text: You mentioned the term "abnormal".
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I wouldn't agree that this is an abnormal finding, even if that was confirmed to be a true finding --
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- because we see it very often in babies. We see it in adults. The only complication this may have is a complication called volvulus. So because it has this course, the membrane that connects that to the walls of the abdomen, we all have that membrane, called the mesocolon, that's the name of the membrane, that membrane is larger because it has a larger distance from the wall to cover. This allows for the colon to twist around itself when we are digesting, for example. This twisting around itself is called volvulus.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Complications of volvulus could be the baby or the adult starts to vomit or not producing any stool, they are in severe pain, they have a fever, and on naked eye examination you will see that bowel. I tend to say to my registrars, "If you miss a volvulus on naked eye, you should not be passing your exams". It's something you don't miss. It's obvious. blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: So as I said earlier, on the histology examination there was evidence of acute pneumonia with acute lung injury on the histology from [Baby C]. blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: A baby with pneumonia responding to treatment, this is the expertise of the neonatologist, the descriptions we pathologists
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: And so that eventuality fits with the stomach being dilated on the basis that the air passes from the stomach immediately into the small bowel? Am I with you so far?

blocks.text: That's correct.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So bearing that in mind as well, what did you then move on to --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I said, okay, let's examine this possibility being the truth. What are the potential explanations for that?
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So one is deliberate exogenous administration of air via the tube. That's one explanation.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The other explanation is necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Sorry?

blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Okay. So that's --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's possibility 1. And we parked the CPAP --
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- in possibility 1.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So leave the CPAP to one side?

blocks.text: Yes, all right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay?
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So this is -- is this in -- sorry to stop you again, but is this -- and to be contrasted to the -- possibility number 1 was small bowel distended, this is possibility number 2, large bowel distended?

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So the distended colon; yes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. And it's on the left side that I see it on the photographs. That's where I see the distended bowel loops. So I was thinking, could this distension correlate to that description?
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And again, I had to make a logical approach of what that meant. So you need to understand a mechanism, how air would be in the proximal aspect of a canal, so in the entry of a tunnel; that's the stomach. There is no dispute there's air in there. It's seen on photographs, it's seen at post-mortem examination, it's seen on radiology. And the proximal part of the small bowel, the duodenum, again there is no dispute on that.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Then there is no air in between and there is air on the distal part. That's what I had to explain, should this have been the case.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So I had to break that down, bearing in mind that would have been a very unusual distribution of air in a bowel to make logical sense. So what would explain this biphasic, if I call it this way, distribution of air in a bowel? It could be an infection that had a localised effect in the two areas, or disseminated infection, sepsis, that, for a weird and wonderful reason that I cannot explain, presented itself this way. There is no evidence of infection on histology, there's no evidence of infection, of sepsis on histology, and the clinical presentation was what I explained.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So I had to consider: what about that pneumonia?
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Would that pneumonia direct your thought that there is a systematic infection going on that could present like that? So should that have been the case, one would expect some other findings. A body's response to a systematic infection rather than a localised infection would be either a systemic inflammatory response or a response with molecules that are in the blood called chemokines. Okay? So the part with chemokines
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: and interleukins and all those molecules I cannot assess on post-mortem but the clinical indication that the baby was stable and responding to treatment makes this unlikely. So that's one mechanism part.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: The other mechanism, the morphologically evident systemic inflammatory response to an infection I know is there in the body. What would pathologists look for?
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: They would look for histological evidence of such a response in the liver. I'm more than happy to go into the details of those findings if you want me.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Were they there?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They were not there.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: That may do.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So considering those possibilities, liver histology, bone marrow histology, spleen histology, capillaries of the other organs, was there any systemic inflammatory -- there was nothing there to suggest that this baby had a systemic response to the localised infection. So that possibility to explain the air presence in the bowel -- again, I had no findings to suggest it. I think I can reasonably exclude it.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Then we go to other finding, other conditions, like volvulus, twisting of the small bowel or twisting of the large bowel. I have explained previously why this cannot be a volvulus because the colour is normal, there is no twisting, there is nothing on histology.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: The other possibility is a condition called Hirschsprung's disease, which is a condition where the nerves, small cells in the wall of the bowel, are absent, and it's typically the large bowel, so the distal part, the part of potential interest here.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: I looked under the microscope. The cells were there, so we cannot suggest Hirschsprung's disease in this.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So having considered all this, I came to the conclusion that most likely the description about the descending and sigmoid was imprecise and what we were looking at were dilated stomach and bowel.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Which would be in keeping with the radiology?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Which would be in keeping with the radiology. And having excluded, as far as I could, all the proposed conditions, we have not discussed CPAP yet, barely.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: No, we haven't discussed post-mortem gas either.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Having not yet discussed CPAP and post-mortem decomposition, the distribution of air would be in keeping with injection of air through the tube.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So CPAP --
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Can we deal with decomposition first? I'm sorry to divert you, but it may be more straightforward. I'm looking at your paragraph 8(b)(vi).
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: Can you exclude post-mortem decomposition as the source of the gas that was found?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Um... Highly, highly unlikely. The description of the bowel is that of a normal bowel. That's how it looks in post-mortem. There were no microscopic findings to suggest that decomposition was of any significance there. But most importantly, on the sampled segments of the bowel that I looked at, on histology, the mucosa, the inner surface of the bowel, not the outer surface, that's the first thing that will go into decomposition, looked normal. So yes, I think I can confidently exclude it instead of just saying highly unlikely, yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: All right. Having excluded all other possibilities, what about CPAP?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So CPAP -- and I need to express myself with caution here because I'm not the expert on how CPAP actually works in babies. My understanding is it's used in millions of babies and it's a safe procedure in neonatal care units.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: My understanding is that the clinicians felt that it is unlikely that CPAP would explain this dilatation.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: My experience as a pathologist dealing with neonates and dealing with neonatal care unit doctors discussing cases -- in my experience, from reading the literature and textbooks, and going back to the cases to see, I've never come across a description or a suggestion of CPAP belly accounting for arrest of a baby, nor have I been asked by any of my colleagues at St Thomas', "Could this be a possibility?" So I think it's fairly, highly unlikely that CPAP belly would explain this distribution of air.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So as opposed to the possibility that somebody put air down the nasogastric tube and caused what was found -- I'm looking now at your (xi) -- were you left with what you regarded as a theoretical possible alternative?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So something trapping the air, which resolved and left the trapped air there, despite the fact it wasn't there to trap it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. That's a very theoretical possibility. I have never come across such a description. I have never seen it. I cannot think of a reasonably plausible mechanism, but I consider it as a theoretical possibility.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: All right. Theoretical possibilities apart, what was your opinion as to why it was that [Baby C] died when he did?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: On the basis of what I have explained and the information, I think that the explanation for the sudden collapse in a background of his pneumonia was the excessive injection or infusion of air into the tube.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Hyaline membranes. blocks.text: One is the physical presence of the neutrophils there, they block the exchange. Two is, if you remember I discussed those cells that form the lining of the alveoli, the air spaces --

blocks.text: In premature babies, especially when they have been born in the context of hypoxia related to the delivery or in utero hypoxia or infection around the time of delivery, you have reduced either blood flow or oxygen supply, in most cases in babies it's a reduced oxygen supply to the brain, which results in areas of the brain dying.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: So the very acute changes one can see are the so-called hypoxic neurons that we see in specific areas of the brain and for those to be visible you need -- depending on the textbook one chooses to rely on, some textbooks will say 2 to 6 hours, some will say 4 to 6 hours from the onset of hypoxia. So you have hypoxia, you need 2 to 4 -- sorry, 4 to 6 or 2 to 6 hours for that very early change to become visible. If the baby dies that the point, you see it. If the baby dies before, you don't see it.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: If the baby survives from the onset of hypoxia, the changes because of the reduced oxygen supply evolve.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: And in the evolvement of that hypoxia you have changes around these ventricles that are inside the brain and it's basically areas, small areas, which may become bigger later on if the baby survives, and that's what we see in babies that have cerebral palsy, for example, and live.
blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: You have areas where the baby's brains, small areas where the parenchyma is dead and that, when the time goes on, will become something like a cyst and that cyst may be filled with water -sorry, with fluid, cerebrospinal fluid, and remain like this. blocks.speaker: MARNERIDES

blocks.text: What this doctor described is changes around the ventricles that tells us that there has been a hypoxic ischaemic event to this brain weeks ago.
